hr1-the-standard-before-the-claim.reason: Opens on 1 Thessalonians 5:21 and the Bereans; the sorting into fact, frame and judgment comes in the third paragraph, and the lesson ends on the course's stance, not on which claim you are testing.
hr1-the-standard-before-the-claim.open: THE QUESTION IN THE TITLE. Before you argue about America's founding, which claim are you testing? First get the claim exactly right, in the maker's own words. Then sort it. A claim of fact (a ship, a date, a number) can be answered by a record. A claim of frame (which year to call the founding) can only be judged by whether it helps you see the records. A claim of judgment (about motives) must be tested against what people wrote and did. Here is how the Word sets that order.
hr1-the-standard-before-the-claim.close: BACK TO THE QUESTION. Which claim are you actually testing? Find out before you argue. Quote the claim in the maker's own words. Then ask what kind it is: a fact a record can settle, a frame that can only be judged by what it helps you see, or a judgment about motives that must be weighed against what the founders wrote and did. The simple believe every word (Proverbs 14:15); the prudent sort first. Only Yahweh's word is true before any record is opened. Everything else is proved.

teen.open: Before you argue about history, ask: what exactly is being claimed? Some claims are facts, some are a way of looking at things, and some are judgments about why people acted.
teen.close: So the first step is to know which kind of claim you are testing. Facts get checked against records. Ways of looking get judged by what they help you see. Judgments get tested against what people really said and did.

senior.open: The title asks which claim one is testing before debating the founding. The lesson's answer is to quote the claim exactly and sort it, since a claim of fact, a claim of frame and a claim of judgment are each tested differently.
senior.close: So the answer is that no argument is sound until the claim is named and sorted. A record answers a fact; a frame is judged by what it reveals or hides; a judgment of motive is weighed against what people wrote and did. Only the Word is true before the record is opened.

hr1-go-to-the-record.open: THE QUESTION IN THE TITLE. What does the nearest record really prove about 1619? That in August 1619 a ship reached Point Comfort, Virginia, carrying about twenty enslaved Africans who were sold to the colonists, believed to be the first in British North America. On that fact the project is accurate. The nearest witness of all, John Rolfe's eyewitness letter, has not yet been fetched, so the course does not quote it. Here is the method behind that answer.
hr1-go-to-the-record.close: BACK TO THE QUESTION. What does the nearest record prove about 1619, and what is still unopened? The fetched records establish the landing: a ship at Point Comfort in August 1619, about twenty enslaved Africans sold to the colonists, the first such landing in British North America as the project and its own fact-checker state it. The project is right on that fact. Rolfe's letter is the record still to be opened, and until it is, it is not quoted (Proverbs 18:13). State each fact at exactly the strength its record gives.

teen.open: What do we actually know about the ship that came to Virginia in 1619? The records show it brought about twenty enslaved Africans who were sold there.
teen.close: So the record proves the landing, and the project got that fact right. One eyewitness letter has not been read yet, so we do not guess what it says. We only say what the records show.

senior.open: The title asks what the nearest record proves about 1619. The fetched records establish a landing at Point Comfort that August of about twenty enslaved Africans sold to the colonists, and the project states that fact accurately.
senior.close: So the answer is that the landing stands, at the strength the records give it, and the project is right on it. John Rolfe's eyewitness letter remains the record not yet opened, and an honest researcher will not quote what he has not read.

hr1-the-witnesses.reason: Why Yahweh hears them first (Genesis 4:10, Psalms 9:12) is answered in the opening; the lesson ends on 'read one of them whole' rather than landing what the four witnesses showed and why it matters.
hr1-the-witnesses.open: THE QUESTION IN THE TITLE. What did Equiano, Jacobs, Douglass and Wells write, and why does Yahweh hear them first? They wrote what slavery did to them, in their own words: a child stolen from home, a father who could never buy his children, an aunt whipped until covered with blood, lynchings counted by name. Yahweh hears them first because He hears the wronged directly and does not forget the cry of the humble (Psalms 9:12). Here are their own words.
hr1-the-witnesses.close: BACK TO THE QUESTION. Why does Yahweh hear these four voices first? Because He hears the cry of the wronged directly and remembers it, and His verdict against stealing and selling a man was given long before any history was written (Exodus 21:16). Equiano, Jacobs, Douglass and Wells supply what a summary leaves out: the testimony, dated and in their own hands. A researcher who leaves them out has left out what Yahweh attends to first. So read one of them whole.

teen.open: Four people who lived through slavery wrote down what happened to them. Yahweh hears people who are hurt like that first, and He does not forget them.
teen.close: So their voices matter most, because Yahweh listens to them first. Read one of their stories all the way through, and you will see what a short summary leaves out.

senior.open: The title asks what four witnesses wrote and why Yahweh hears them first. They recorded slavery in their own hands, and Scripture shows Yahweh attends directly to the cry of the wronged (Genesis 4:10; Psalms 9:12).
senior.close: So the answer is that the people slavery was done to are the first witnesses, because Yahweh hears them first. His verdict was given before any research; their testimony shows, in their own words, what that verdict was given for.

hr1-fact-and-interpretation.reason: Method and verses first; the finding (the three facts under the claim do not hold, so it cannot stand as printed; some colonists' motives remain a case-by-case question) comes in the fifth paragraph.
hr1-fact-and-interpretation.open: THE QUESTION IN THE TITLE. Did the colonists declare independence to protect slavery? Not as the essay printed it. The claim rested on three facts, and historians with the record in hand showed each one does not hold, so the claim cannot stand as printed. Some colonists did want to protect slavery, and how far that moved particular men is answered case by case. You test a case like this by testing each fact under it. Here is how.
hr1-fact-and-interpretation.example: ONE FACT, TESTED. Take the essay's second fact: that in London there were growing calls to abolish the slave trade. The researcher's question is simple: when did that movement begin? Wilentz answers from the record that it formed only in 1787. The Declaration was 1776. So that support is eleven years too late to be a cause, and it comes out from under the claim. Do the same with the other two facts, and you see what is left standing.
hr1-fact-and-interpretation.close: BACK TO THE QUESTION. Did the colonists declare independence to protect slavery? The essay said it was a primary reason, and its three supporting facts failed against the record, so the claim cannot stand as printed. What survives is narrower: some colonists did want to protect slavery, a question the record answers one case at a time. And that is how you test any historian's case: quote the claim, list its facts, test each with a named witness, and restate it at the strength that survives (Exodus 23:1).

teen.open: Did America declare independence to protect slavery? The essay said so, but the facts it leaned on did not hold up when historians checked them.
teen.close: So the big claim cannot stand as it was printed. Some colonists did want to protect slavery, but that is a smaller claim. To test any claim, check each fact under it, one at a time.

senior.open: The title asks whether the colonists declared independence to protect slavery. As printed, no: the three facts under that interpretation were each answered from the record and did not hold.
senior.close: So the answer is that the claim falls as printed, while the narrower truth stands: some colonists wanted slavery protected, a matter settled case by case. The method is the lasting gain: quote, list the facts, test each against a named witness, and restate what survives.

hr1-two-or-three-witnesses-the-process.reason: The answer (the process was closed; Harris disputed the claim before print and was not heeded; leading scholars were not asked) is only given in the final verdict paragraph after four witnesses.
hr1-two-or-three-witnesses-the-process.open: THE QUESTION IN THE TITLE. Did the 1619 Project check its claim before printing? It asked, but it did not heed the answer. Its own fact-checker, Leslie Harris, disputed the claim about why the colonists declared independence, and the magazine printed it anyway. Leading historians of the period say they were never approached, and five historians called the process closed. The two-witness rule was not kept. Here is the testimony.
hr1-two-or-three-witnesses-the-process.close: BACK TO THE QUESTION. Did the 1619 Project check its claim before printing? By the words of the people inside the process, not in the way Deuteronomy 19:15 requires. One qualified witness disputed the claim and was not heeded, the scholars who could have searched it were not asked, and five historians called the process closed. The aim was serious; the check failed. The lesson for you is not distrust. It is to build two or three witnesses into your own work before it leaves your hands (Proverbs 12:15).

teen.open: Did the project check its big claim before printing it? Its own fact-checker said the claim was wrong, and they printed it anyway.
teen.close: So the answer is no, not really. They did not listen to the expert they asked. The lesson for you is to let two or three people check your work before you share it.

senior.open: The title asks whether the project checked its claim before publication. By the testimony of those inside the process, the one historian consulted disputed it and was not heeded, and the leading scholars were not asked.
senior.close: So the answer is that the two-witness rule was not kept. The aim was serious, but the process was closed. The remedy is not suspicion of others but building counsel into one's own work before it is published.

hr1-the-correction-and-the-quiet-edit.reason: Says early the magazine changed its record 'both ways', and the ending lands the two disciplines, but obliquely; the close states plainly which change was open and which was silent.
hr1-the-correction-and-the-quiet-edit.close: BACK TO THE QUESTION. Did the magazine admit its mistake, or quietly erase it? Both. In March 2020 it openly corrected one sentence, with a note, names and a date, so that all became some. Separately, the language calling 1619 the true founding disappeared from the page with no note, as a columnist at the same paper reported, and only a dated copy could show it. That is how you tell them apart: an open correction is named, explained and dated; a silent edit leaves no note. So keep dated copies, and when your own words change, tell your reader.

teen.open: When a magazine fixes a mistake, does it tell you? This one did once, out in the open, and once it changed words without saying so.
teen.close: So the answer is both. An honest fix is named and dated. A quiet edit leaves no note, and only a saved copy shows it. Save copies, and when you fix your own work, say so.

senior.open: The title asks whether the magazine owned its error or erased it. The record shows both: an open correction with names and a date, and a later change made without any note.
senior.close: So the answer is both, and the difference is visible in the record itself. An open correction is named, explained and dated; a silent edit can be seen only against a dated copy. Keep such copies, and correct your own work openly.

hr1-the-city-they-built.reason: Says a city has authors, but who drew the lines (owners' covenants, the FHA's lending maps, local officials routing highways) is spread across five records, and the lesson ends asking the reader to find out.
hr1-the-city-they-built.open: THE QUESTION IN THE TITLE. Who drew the line across your city? People with names and pens. Property owners signed covenants keeping their streets white. The federal housing agency drew lending maps that denied credit by neighborhood. Local officials chose where the interstates ran, and in Atlanta the mayor said one was plotted as a boundary. A city is a stack of decrees with authors, and Yahweh judges the authors (Isaiah 10:1-2). Here are the records.
hr1-the-city-they-built.close: BACK TO THE QUESTION. Who drew the line across your city? The records name them: thirty owners on Labadie Avenue who signed a covenant, the FHA that the Federal Reserve calls the architect of redlining, the officials who routed Interstate 20 as a boundary, and urban renewal that moved families out. Kruse was right, and the government itself now funds the repair. The lines were written, so they can be traced, and what was drawn by decree can be mended. Find yours, ask who drew it, and be a repairer of the breach (Isaiah 58:12).

teen.open: Who decided where the lines in your city go? Real people did, with papers, maps and plans, not by accident.
teen.close: So the answer is that people drew those lines on purpose, and the records show who. Yahweh calls His people to be repairers. Find the line in your city and ask how to help mend it.

senior.open: The title asks who drew the dividing lines in our cities. The records answer that they were drawn by named authors: owners' covenants, federal lending maps, and officials who chose highway routes.
senior.close: So the answer is that the lines were decrees, written and signed, and the government's own records now say so and fund their repair. Yahweh judges unrighteous decrees and calls His people to be repairers of the breach (Isaiah 58:12).

hr1-write-it-in-order-for-our-children.open: THE QUESTION IN THE TITLE. Could a child check every line of history? Yes, when it is written the way this lesson teaches: plain, in order, with a named record under every sentence. A finding a child cannot follow, with its records attached, is not finished. Here is the course’s own finding written that way, and the sight it is meant to give.
hr1-write-it-in-order-for-our-children.close: BACK TO THE QUESTION. Could a child check every line of history? This lesson showed that it can be done. The course’s finding, from the 1619 landing to the corrected sentence to the redlining records, points every line to a record any reader can open, and it keeps both the settled and the narrow in view. Written that way, a child does more than remember a story. He sees a nation measured by the Word, and he is ready to be the repairer of the breach Yahweh calls him to be.

teen.open: Can a kid check every line of history? Yes, if each sentence points to a real record you can open.
teen.close: So yes. Write it plain, put a record under every line, and anyone, even a child, can check it. That is how you see a nation measured by the Word.

senior.open: The title asks whether a child could check every line of history. The answer is yes, when the finding is written plainly, in order, with a named record beneath each sentence.
senior.close: So a child can check every line, provided the writer has done the work: plain words, careful order, and a record under every claim. Such writing lets a young reader see a nation measured by the Word, not the Word measured by a nation.
